This season feels as if its split in half, well an uneven half, but fortunately the second half is pretty superb which helps a ton for the overall impact of this part. The first 8 or so episodes were pretty slow, with the first 2 completely focusing on Eris which I really enjoyed, we haven't seen her for ages and watching her grow to control her aggression but also still keep her feisty personality made her feel a lot more mature and made for a really fun watch surprisingly. After that the show has a bit of a slow point in my opinion, i understand thenuance in developing the characters relationships and their individual growth, but i really wanted the story to pick up the pace a bit so we could see eris and rudeus interact and how that will affect Rudeus' life as a whole.

The season gets to its very dramatic high point in episode 12 and 13.

Episode 12 was really great, the pure dread and desperation future Rudeus displayed gave this episode a type of horror that ive never experienced before, it was really unique!

What i dont like about it though is Rudeus (current) reaction to all of this information, he literally gets like 3 pieces of proof showcasing that this is his future self warning him, then goes to the one place that his future self warned him not to go, and did the one of the only things he was told not to do. The rats footsteps at the basement would be enough proof but he opened the door either way.

Yes im aware he froze the hell out of the basement but when everything he loves is on the line i would of expected him to take it more seriously than 2 ice spells.

On that note actually, Rudeus is kind of boring, as a special super strong one of a kind mage, hes really not all that impressive, i expected alot more from him in his conflict with the demon king lady i forgot her name. Plus! he only uses like 3 spells, electric is new i guess but thats about it, hes been using water and earth for like... well hes probably only like 18 but still.

Diary on the other hand is just a brutal episode all the way through, seeing the current day unfold in just the worst possible way ever was haunting, and all of the domino effects, while convenient for the plot, where horrible to see in the best way possible.

All in all it was a solid part with an exciting finish leading us onto the second cour, see you there!

entry.title: Seihantai na Kimi to Boku 2nd Season

data.review:
From the annals of "WTF did I just watch?" comes the third season of A Certain Magical Index, which is not really the third installment of the franchise because the story threads into other shows. If you've made it this far you've probably invested a LOT of time into these characters. Sadly, it will not be rewarded. Index mostly disappears from her own show and she's not even replaced by other beloved characters like Misaka and her clones. Instead you get an onslaught of characters you don't know or care about dumping exposition like there's no tomorrow, dragging you through one meaningless struggle after theother. Even Last Order gets the cold storage treatment and Accelerator responds by getting cringe. You can skip this entire season and go straight to the third season of A Certain Scientific Railgun.

I slogged through this mess because I've fallen in love with the Misaka Network clones and absolutely need to see every moment they are on screen. The only other reason I can imagine someone watching it is if they are autistic (although to be fair, if you are autistic, then you are probably in love with the Misaka Network clones like me).

The background art is also good with plenty of refreshing scenery that takes place in the snowy forests of Russia. It meets the high standard set by previous seasons.

This was not cynically made. Someone really tried to make this good. The final episodes even provide some level of catharsis for all the difficult moments you had to put up with to get there. It just wasn't enough for me.

Look, I know this show is totally male age gap fantasy, but the main couple is so cute together that I can't help but love it. And yes, I see plain as day that it's a trap for introverted 40-something male anime fans, but I don't care because it's executed so damn well. I crave escapism and Yamada-chan doth provide. After laboring through the endless droves of high-school-centric romance animes, shows like this that focus on older chararcters in the workplace are always refreshing to me. Even better is the fact that even though you could call this a romcom, it doesn't dwell in cheap hackycomedy (except the Obata episode. The Obata episode sucks.) and really does the romance part right. It doesn't tell you how to feel as much as it just lets you come along for the ride.

The male protaganist Sasaki is the biggest golden retriever character ever. The show even directly says so. Yet, he manages to do exactly the right thing at exactly the right time whenever it's needed. It really hammers home the chemistry between the wise older man and the playfulness of the younger woman that works so well in this series. 

I think one of the things that makes this show great is that it cuts out everything in the character's lives that isn't important. The editing is superb. You get a few of Sasaki's work dilemmas, and a rare shot of Yamada outside of the supermarket, but other than that it's all just focused on their conversations and what they're feeling in the moment. Absolutely nothing is filler. Many of the side characters barely get developed, but it feels very purposeful and not flawed at all.  The background characters don't even get the luxury of having eyes.

I did think it was odd that they switched out the super catchy ending theme Night Dancer that was used in the mini-episodes for a still catchy but much less so song from Imase for the full episodes. I can only assume it was a push by Imase's label. The opening theme I found quite skippable aside from the obligatory first and last episode where I make a ritual of never skipping anything.

The show's attitudes surrounding smoking and health are pretty hilariously at points. I won't spoil it, but there's an episode around mid-season that just has the most ass-backwards way of looking at one's health that it should be given some ridicule. But I suppose whatever's clever when it keeps you from having to stop talking to the cute girl who's half your age. Also, waking up before dawn just to purposefully smoke in the freezing cold is peak health.

I'd like to talk about the ending more but it would wind up being spoiler territory. I just know that while it wasn't what I was expecting, it still felt good in it's own way. I think they were just being careful not to wreck anything and I would say they achieved that gracefully.

Anyways, this show is straight up adorable. Watching Sasaki and Yamada slowly losing the battle of playing dodgeball with their feelings is completely addictive. You may ask yourself things like "Why doesn't a super attractive girl like Yamada have tons of other people in her life?" but just ignore those silly rational thoughts and have fun watching this banger of a series for what it is: a great romantic comedy. If this doesn't get another season I might die inside.

9/10

entry.title: Super no Ura de Yani Suu Futari

data.review:
This isn't a particular review but just my thoughts on this show and this have all the spoilers of the show so please don't read before completing it. It’s difficult to put my thoughts about Oreimo into words. On the surface, it starts like a pretty typical anime: a sister who hates her brother, a brother who doesn’t understand his sister, and two people who seem incapable of getting along. Generally, I’m not a fan of characters who force themselves to hate someone, especially when their reasons for doing so aren’t properly explored. But something about Oreimo felt different. Maybe it was because I already knewabout its infamous reputation, or maybe there was something genuinely unique about it that I couldn’t quite put my finger on.
Throughout Season 1, I kept thinking, Wow, what a show! It had been a while since I’d watched something this entertaining. The anime pulled me into its universe, made me invest in its characters, and eventually reached a point where I couldn’t stop thinking about it even when I wasn’t watching. That, to me, is one of the most important things a story can accomplish.
One thing I particularly admire about Oreimo is how it balances comedy with a drama-driven storyline. That combination is surprisingly difficult to pull off. A show can be funny without having anything meaningful to say, and it can be emotionally profound without necessarily being entertaining. Oreimo somehow manages to do both. Take the scene where Kyousuke discovers Kirino’s interest in erotic games featuring little-sister characters. Instead of simply judging her or telling her that her hobby is wrong, he stands up for her, even when it means confronting their father and facing the consequences himself. That entire confrontation deserves a round of applause. How the hell can a scene be so funny while simultaneously having something genuinely deep to say?
Let’s be honest: we all have our weird hobbies and interests. Some might be embarrassing, some might be difficult to explain, and others might seem downright bizarre to people who don’t share them. But as long as our interests aren’t hurting anyone, why should we be shamed for them? And I’ll admit something here: I’m pretty sure I’ve judged other people for their interests at some point in my life, simply because I didn’t understand them. Looking back, I’m genuinely sorry for that. This scene reminded me that sometimes, all you need is one person who understands you. Someone who doesn’t necessarily share your interests but is willing to listen, understand, and stand beside you when everyone else is judging you. Sometimes, that one person can make all the difference.
For me, one of the biggest strengths of Oreimo is its character dynamics. Most of the relationships feel surprisingly natural, with people taking time to understand one another rather than instantly becoming best friends. Ironically, the main character is probably the exception, considering how many characters eventually develop feelings for him.
Kirino’s difficulty in finding friends was something I could relate to. It’s not always easy to find people who share your interests, especially when those interests are relatively niche. Having nobody to discuss something you genuinely love can feel isolating. For me, that feeling became easier to understand once TMC came along. What I particularly liked about Kirino and Kuroneko was that they didn’t immediately become friends. Their relationship took time to develop, and they initially connected through something anime fans know all too well: arguing about their favourite shows and defending their opinions as though their lives depended on it. I genuinely loved their dynamic. They finally had someone who understood what it meant to be passionate about something that others might not appreciate. That’s why their first major disagreement felt so satisfying. For once, they had someone who cared enough about the same things to argue with them. Sometimes, an argument isn't a sign that a relationship is falling apart; it can be a sign that both people finally feel comfortable enough to be themselves. Beneath all their arguments, I think Kirino and Kuroneko understood each other more deeply than either of them realised.
Kirino and Ayase, on the other hand, had a completely different dynamic. Their relationship gave me yuri vibes, almost as though Ayase might have romantic feelings for Kirino. Her protectiveness and emotional reactions made their interactions interesting to watch, and I sometimes found myself wondering whether their relationship was intended to be interpreted that way. Regardless, it was another example of how the show gave different characters distinct relationships rather than making everyone interact with Kirino and Kyousuke in exactly the same way.
Then there’s Manami. The way Kyousuke describes her sometimes makes her sound almost like a grandmother, which is particularly ironic considering that she has feelings for him. Yet, Manami consistently remains by his side. Her affection isn't particularly flashy or dramatic; she is familiar, dependable, and present even when she doesn't receive the same attention as the other girls. I also wish Manami’s grandfather had received more screen time. I absolutely loved him. He was one of those characters who could make an impression without needing to dominate the story, and I genuinely wanted to see more of him.
Saori is another character I appreciate, although perhaps for a different reason. She might not be central to the main storyline, but she somehow brings everyone together. She creates the circumstances in which these characters can meet, interact, and form relationships. She might not always be at the centre of the drama, but she contributes significantly to the atmosphere of the show. Sometimes, a character doesn't need to be the most complex or emotionally significant person in the story. They can be valuable simply because of what they bring out in everyone else. Saori does precisely that.
When it comes to the ending of Season 1, I understand why some people might prefer the good ending, but I personally prefer the true ending because it fits Kirino’s character much better. Kirino has always been a dreamer. She is ambitious, stubborn, and willing to work incredibly hard for what she wants. When an opportunity comes along that could help her achieve her dreams, I can absolutely see her taking it, even if doing so means leaving behind the people she loves. Personally, I’ve never been particularly fond of stories in which a character is expected to abandon their dreams for the sake of love. Love is important, but it shouldn't automatically mean sacrificing your ambitions or giving up on the life you want to build. Kirino pursuing her dreams felt right to me because it wasn't necessarily about loving Kyousuke any less; it was about choosing to pursue something that mattered deeply to her. The OVA later shows Kyousuke going after Kirino and bringing her back when he realises that she isn't quite the same. I wouldn't call that sequence extraordinary, but I appreciated what it demonstrated about their relationship. Their bond had become something substantial, something that could survive distance and separation.
When Season 2 begins, one of the biggest developments is Kyousuke's relationship with Kuroneko. Although their relationship is relatively short-lived, I found it genuinely sweet. For once, Kyousuke seemed to have a relationship that wasn't defined entirely by his complicated dynamic with Kirino. Kuroneko had feelings for him, and there was something satisfying about seeing those feelings develop into an actual relationship. Naturally, I was sad when they broke up. I genuinely wanted things to work out between them. But then came one of the best scenes in the entire series: Kyousuke asking Kirino for a life consultation. And Kuroneko's drawing made the situation even more heartbreaking. The drawing expressed a wish that all three of them could remain together, rather than Kyousuke and Kuroneko dating while Kirino was left on the sidelines. It was such a revealing moment because it showed that Kuroneko's feelings for Kirino went beyond their rivalry and shared interest in anime. She genuinely cared about her. Kuroneko was willing to imagine a world in which she didn't get everything she wanted romantically if it meant preserving the bond between the three of them. There is something painfully human about that. Sometimes, we love someone enough to want them in our lives even when the circumstances aren't ideal for us. That scene made me wish the story had spent even more time exploring the relationship between Kirino and Kuroneko.
Throughout Season 1 and the first OVA, one major complaint I had was that I wanted the story to explore Kirino's perspective more deeply. We saw her behaviour, her arguments, her jealousy, and her reactions to Kyousuke, but I wanted to understand what was happening inside her head. Why was she so hostile towards her brother? What had changed between them? And why did their relationship seem so much more complicated than it initially appeared? Eventually, the story gives us more insight into their childhood. Kirino and Kyousuke were once extremely close, but as they grew older, Kyousuke began to distance himself from her. Kirino, who wasn't quite capable of reaching him in the way she wanted, started working harder, trying to become someone he would notice and admire.
Then she discovered those erotic games featuring little-sister characters. I think this is where things become particularly interesting. The discovery may have forced Kirino to confront feelings and ideas about her brother that she didn't know how to process. Combined with her already complicated relationship with him, it created an emotional situation she couldn't easily understand or express. The confrontation between Kirino and Manami about loving a sibling also adds another layer to this interpretation, forcing Kirino to confront the nature of her feelings and what they might mean. One possible interpretation is that Kirino's tsundere behaviour became a way of dealing with feelings she couldn't openly acknowledge. Instead of expressing affection, she became hostile. Instead of admitting that she wanted to be close to Kyousuke, she acted as though she couldn't stand him.
But I think there is another layer to it. Kirino wasn't simply upset that Kyousuke had grown distant; she was also upset because her image of him was changing. The brother she had admired and depended on was becoming someone she could no longer understand. She wanted to reach him, but she didn't know how. Then, through the events surrounding her secret hobby, Kyousuke once again demonstrated that he was willing to stand by her. He hadn't necessarily become the person she feared he had become. He could still be dependable, and he could still understand her. That realisation seems important to their relationship.
I also have a personal interpretation of why Kirino insisted that Kyousuke play those games with her. Perhaps she wanted to explore or accept a particular kind of relationship through fiction before confronting what it meant in reality. Perhaps she wanted to test his reactions, understand his perspective, or simply create a private world that belonged to the two of them. I can't say that this is definitively what the story intended, but it is an interpretation that makes their interactions more interesting to me. And that's something I appreciate about the series: it gives you enough material to think about the characters beyond their immediate actions, even when it doesn't always explain everything explicitly.
Now, let's talk about my biggest complaints. Why on earth do so many girls end up falling in love with Kyousuke? I can understand Manami. I can understand Kuroneko. Their relationships with him have enough history and development to make their feelings believable. But Ayase? And Kanako? I struggled to understand those relationships. It sometimes felt as though the story was pushing these characters towards Kyousuke because the narrative wanted to fulfil the expectations of the harem genre. Rather than allowing every romantic development to emerge naturally from the characters and their interactions, the show occasionally seemed determined to make Kyousuke the centre of everyone's romantic attention. And that's frustrating because the series is at its strongest when its characters feel like actual people with their own motivations, insecurities, and relationships. Not every girl needs to fall for the protagonist. Sometimes, a character can have an important role in a story without developing romantic feelings for the main character. In fact, I think Oreimo could have benefited from allowing some of these relationships to remain platonic. It would have made the romantic developments that did occur feel more meaningful.
Another complaint is the pacing. A lot happens, and sometimes the story jumps between events so quickly that I wanted more time to process what had just occurred. However, I think this criticism is somewhat debatable. The show doesn't always spell out the characters' feelings directly. Instead, it often relies on their interactions, behaviour, and the surrounding circumstances to communicate what they are experiencing. That approach can be rewarding because it encourages the viewer to interpret the characters rather than simply accept an explanation handed to them. But it can also make certain developments feel abrupt, particularly when the story moves on before giving them the attention they deserve.
Now we arrive at the ending. I know that many people hate it, and I understand why. I don't think the criticism is entirely unjustified. But after finishing the series, I spent around three days thinking about it, and I eventually realised that I genuinely liked the ending. Not because it was perfect, not because every character received the outcome they deserved, and certainly not because it was a particularly comfortable conclusion. I liked it because, in its own controversial way, it felt true to the emotional direction of the story.
Oreimo is a story filled with complicated feelings, difficult choices, jealousy, affection, and heartbreak. It explores relationships that don't always fit neatly into the categories society expects them to occupy. Its characters want things they don't necessarily know how to express, and they make decisions that can hurt the people around them. The ending doesn't magically resolve all those complications. Instead, it commits to the direction the story has been building towards, even when that direction is uncomfortable.
And that matters to me. Love doesn't always reward you. You can love someone deeply and still lose them. You can do your best to understand someone and still hurt them. You can have genuine feelings for another person without those feelings producing a happy, conventional ending. Sometimes, you love someone even when you know that the outcome might not be what you want. That's what makes the ending bittersweet for me.
I also appreciate that the story doesn't attempt to escape the implications of its own premise by relying on some convenient revelation that suddenly makes everything acceptable. It doesn't simply introduce a loophole or rewrite the characters' relationship to make the conclusion easier to swallow. Instead, it leaves us to confront the relationship that the story has actually presented. I won't pretend that this makes every decision in the ending good writing, nor does it mean that everyone should like it. But I respect a story that commits to its central emotional conflict rather than backing away at the last moment simply because the audience might disapprove.
That said, I have one final complaint: the ending was rushed. I genuinely believe Oreimo could have benefited from another season. There were relationships that deserved more development, emotional consequences that needed more time to breathe, and characters whose perspectives I wanted to explore further. The ending might have been more satisfying if the series had given us additional time to understand how everyone arrived at that point. Perhaps that wouldn't have changed the outcome, but it would have made the journey feel more complete.
Looking back, I think I liked Oreimo so much because it dared to explore a kind of love story that many other stories would avoid altogether. It took an uncomfortable, controversial premise and built a story around the people involved in it. Sometimes it handled that premise brilliantly; sometimes it relied too heavily on harem conventions, rushed developments, or convenient romantic progression. But at its best, it made me laugh, sympathise with its characters, question their decisions, and reflect on my own understanding of relationships.
More importantly, it reminded me how much it matters to have someone who understands you. Someone who doesn't immediately judge your interests. Someone who listens even when they don't agree with you. Someone who stands beside you when the rest of the world makes you feel as though there's something wrong with you. That idea might sound simple, but I think it's one of the most meaningful things the series has to offer.
As for my rating, I'm genuinely conflicted. If I were being strictly practical about the writing, pacing, character development, and inconsistencies, I'd probably give it a 7/10 at best. But if I listened to my heart, it would be a 9/10 without much hesitation. The fact that I spent three days thinking about the ending, that I became so invested in these characters, and that the show made me reflect on things beyond the screen means something to me.
So, I'll settle on an 8/10.
Maybe it isn't a perfect anime. Maybe its flaws are too significant for me to call it a masterpiece without qualification. But it is a show that made me feel something, challenged some of my assumptions, and stayed with me long after I finished watching it. And sometimes, that's worth more than a technically perfect story.
Oreimo might not be an anime I can defend on every front, but it's certainly one I won't forget anytime soon.

entry.title: Ore no Imouto ga Konnani Kawaii Wake ga Nai. Specials

data.review:
Sheer garbage. This won't be a thorough review looking at every little aspect because there's no point whatsoever considering how ungodly trash the overall product is. Spoilers for everything, because nothing matters to the show itself, so why should it for you. The premise of the show is already dubious but that's not bad in and of itself. Sure, a 14 year old sold as a slave (basically) to repay a debt, in order to become the wife of this 18 year old, is way more than a little weird (and from a cursory search on google, not even remotely normal for 19 fucking 20s Japan, butthat's besides the point). I'm willing to suspend my disbelief at the paedophile undertones of an anime if they can do anything fun or interesting with it (goodness knows there's precious little to watch without something along those lines these days).

Here's what this show does with those undertones: NOTHING.

Nothing is also just a theme for this shitshow, in general. This show has an absolute fetish for dropping massive issues or problems on the viewers and then just...leaving them. No explanation, no solving of the issues...nothing.
Perfect case in point: the father of the girl thief. We get to know that the mother of this little shithead and of her brothers is dead (of course) and the father tried to make her become a prostitute and then forces her to steal in order to drink away the money she gets home. You might rightly think, even as an average MAL user, "wow, how will they solve that problem?" and here's the funny thing about that...

They don't!

I'm not being facetious or anythig else, they literally do-not-care. Their drunkard abusive "let's have my only female daughter become a prostitute" father just...keeps on living and supposedly beating his children every day for the rest of his life, for all we know and all the anime cares to tell us. And it's hardly the only one. So many situations presented as important just wink away off screen, never to be discussed again. One of the brothers of said joyous family gets hired as a something-or-other in Tokyo and almost-prostitute-turned-thief girl (I can't remember he name and I sure as hell am not going to look it up, she has no character anyway, I'll refer to her as APTT from now on) has a logical reason to want to travel to Tokyo with the main protagonist when an earthquake hits it because, you know, her otouuuuuto is there and she has to find him.

Do we know if she finds him? Actually, we do. How? Because he's present in one of the final cutscenes. Because APPARENTLY her motivation (you know, little brother might be dead, burned alive, gravely injured or whatever else) was good enough to get APTT to Tokyo but not good enough to make whoever came up with this garbage script to decide to focus on that for all of 10 seconds for a clear resolution to such a major point. It's weird af to see her just get around with her usual braindead-induced-smile and being like...are you alright? Weren't you looking for your little brother? Do you just want to bang the protagonist or what (yes, she actually mentions that a few times during this show)?

Speaking of the protagonist...my god, what a useless piece of garbage he is. Tragic backstory, he got injured and lost the use of his right arm (except when using a bicycle and a variety of other situations in which they just forget about his menomation) in an accident in which his mother died (of course). His father and his whole family are horrible people (of course) and tell him he's better to be thought of as dead for them and send him away to some remote village to live in a massive mansion by himself when he literally can't do ANYTHING by himself, he's an Asmongold-level "I'll just live with my roaches" type of guy. He's there for all of 2 weeks before his slave is sent to him and then she can cheerfully do everything he's never spent a single moment doing. #lifehacks!
So, just from this you might think damn, not a good start for a character and yeah, you'd be right. That wouldn't be a negative if the character had growth or changed substantially; plenty of characters start off as insufferable whiners and yet a few of them actually become decent and even likable.
Needless to say, he's not part of that prestigious group. He starts the anime whining about how he'd rather be dead, how he'd rather not live, how he's hated and blahblahblahblah (and when I say whining, I do MEAN whining, this guy is an 8 year old when it comes to that, absolutely insufferable) and he's like that basically until the second to last episode. He remains a completely unadjusted useless human being, who does nothing for his slave, pardon, wife-to-be, except complain about how he's not worthy of marrying her (aw, how cute) and sulking like a fucking toddler when he makes her worry after making some insanely batshit mistakes. It's just mind-boggling, I have absolutely no idea who's supposed to find this guy relatable, likable or to have positive feelings stirring in their chests when thinking of this amoeba.

The premise of Seraph of the End is genuinely interesting. Most of the world’s population dies, monsters take over, and the survivors are caught between two factions: vampires, and a Japanese military that partners with demons through ancient rituals. Regular humans are stuck in the crossfire. It’s a solid setup, and it’s what kept me watching for the first half of the series. Unfortunately, the execution doesn’t live up to it. I dropped it at episode 6 because I couldn’t get past how flat the characters are. Whenever they talk to each other, there’s no substance to the conversations, and the emotions feel monotonous. Scenes thatare supposed to carry weight just bored me, and I found myself waiting for the plot to move rather than caring about the people in it.

The main character is the biggest problem. He’s constantly angry and shouting, and it makes him very hard to watch. I understand he’s a teenager, but it’s the same note over and over, and it’s grating on the ears. None of the other characters were interesting enough to make up for it either.

In fairness, the art style and animation are very good, which makes sense since it was animated by Wit Studio. Visually, it’s a strong production.

Maybe I’m spoiled by how modern anime approaches character interactions, since I fail to see how this was so popular in 2015. If you’re older than 13 and like characters with real depth and believable emotional reactions, I doubt you’ll be able to get through this without cringing every few minutes. Viewers who just want a dark-fantasy premise with action and don’t mind shallow characters might enjoy it more than I did, but it wasn’t for me.

Some love stories are not simply about falling in love, but about learning to appreciate life, cherishing the time we have with the people we love, and finding hope even in the darkest moments. Love Unseen Beneath the Clear Night Sky is one such story, a deeply emotional romance that reminds us of the beauty of human connection and the profound impact one person can have on another's life. What makes this story particularly special is the contrast between its two protagonists. Kakeru a regular young man who prefers to keep his distance from others, who lives in an emotional darkness, he is introverted, carries pasttrauma, and feels isolated from the rest of the world, on the other hand Koharu, a young woman who lives in a physical darkness due to her blindness, but has a cheerful, outgoing personality whose positive outlook on life is genuinely infectious. Despite the hardships this girl has faced, she retains her bright personality and manages to bring joy and hope to the people around her, Kakeru included. Her character embodies the idea that, even when life gives us countless reasons to lose hope, we can still find reasons to smile and make others happy. Their relationship develops gradually, allowing us to appreciate the little things that make falling in love so special like the awkwardness of getting closer to someone, the excitement of spending time together, the desire to make the other person happy, and the realization that someone who was once a stranger can eventually become an irreplaceable part of our lives.

Beyond the romance itself, the story explores love in its many forms, showing how caring for someone means more than simply wanting to be with them. Sometimes, it means standing by their side when things become difficult, offering support when words are not enough, and finding the strength to keep moving forward together. 
The emotional weight of the narrative comes from how deeply it understands the importance of these seemingly ordinary moments.
Also, the story does benefit from the fact that it takes place in a university setting instead of the usual recycled high-school romance that relies on the same overused tropes. It takes its time building an emotional connection between its characters, making their relationship feel more personal and meaningful. 
By the way, this is by no means a story for everyone since its emotional approach can be quite heavy, and some developments may feel melodramatic to those who prefer more lighthearted, understanded storytelling. 
Nevertheless, its sincerity is one of its greatest strengths because it genuinely wants the audience to feel something, and it succeeds in making its characters' happiness, struggles, and affection matter.

In the end, Love Unseen Beneath the Clear Night Sky is a heartfelt and bittersweet romance about love, hope, and the importance of cherishing the time we are given. If you enjoy emotional love stories that aim to leave a lasting impression rather than simply provide a feel-good romantic experience, this is a series worth experiencing.

I really want to love Link Click Season 3, I do. Seasons 1 and 2 left such a profound impact on me and made it one of my favorite shows of all time, so I came in with really high hopes. Unfortunately, Season 3 was entrusted to a new studio and director and it shows- while the season is still airing and has a second half that could redeem it, as of right now, this season is failing to reach the heights of its predecessors. This season moves at a breakneck pace without giving the viewer much time to breathe at all, and while thereare emotional moments, they are failing to hit the same highs as previous seasons due to how fast everything is moving. I cried multiple times in previous seasons of Link Click, whereas this season has not even evoked more than a sort of 'aw :(' reaction to big emotional moments. Part of this is also due to the expanding cast of characters who, while interesting and pretty to look at, have spread the show so thin that no one character is getting the attention they truly deserve, and no one is suffering more for it than the main three.

Lu Guang is such a powerful character, and seasons 1 and 2 have spent so much time carefully weaving his story. Unfortunately, it all comes crashing down in season 3. Where Lu Guang is praised for his maturity and composure in previous seasons, he is rapidly losing control over his emotions in season 3- and to an extent, that makes sense, but the shift does not feel "earned". Yes, we know Lu Guang has been through a lot and deserves to break down, but this season is less of a slow decline into that and more of him just falling apart all at once, and it's a sharp tonal shift compared to the character we know. 

Meanwhile, Cheng Xiaoshi feels like he's actively regressed as a character. Previous seasons have taught him a very harsh lesson about how even the smallest changes in the timeline can lead to multiple casualties, and that no matter how much he wants to help, sometimes he just needs to let the past be. That does not show at all here, with him actively ignoring and going against Lu Guang's guidance multiple times and putting those he's possessed in active danger for it. Cheng Xiaoshi is reckless, certainly, but he's far from an idiot. Some of the most well thought-out plans of previous seasons came from him, showing an intelligence and craftiness that is lost in this season. 

There's a lot more I could say, but ultimately, the season isn't over yet and I'm still holding out hope that it will improve- these thoughts just represent my current take on the series and where it's at right now. I think there's still a lot worth seeing in it, but it has a long way to go before it can match the prowess of what came before it.

OVA so good it made me go back to reviewing anime after two years. Despite having been a huge fan of Evangelion for quite some time, I just recently discovered Gunbuster after seeing a GIF on Twitter featuring the show's opening sequence. I admit I wasn't very well-informed about the past works of Hideaki Anno or Gainax in general; all I knew was Evangelion and Kareshi Kanojo no Jijou, and the rest had never really been on my radar. I'm glad I delved deeper into Anno's lesser-known works, as his career in animation has turned out to be more interesting than I expected. Gunbuster (or TWN tomake it short) tells the story of a 15 years old pilot named Noriko whose father Takaya Yuzo tragically died during a battle against alien forces when she was a little kid. She then begins to attend the Okynawa High School, having issues however with piloting big robots despite being an expert in physical exercise. With great determination and encouragement from her coach Ota, not only does she begin to gradually realize her true potential and become a great pilot, but she will also follow her father's footsteps and be the one in charge of piloting the Gunbuster!
So premise wise this series might not sound too impressive for some people, especially for those who aren't particularly into Mecha genre. Admittedly one of the reasons of why I was interested to this OVA to begin with (on top of being Hideaki Anno's directorial debut) was the cast mainly involve high school girls with awesome and attractive "space suits" that are used during the Mech action, which is pretty much the same selling point of Evangelion to me. I found it hard to imagine that this anime would reach the same level of excellence as Eva - a feat the latter achieved not only through its story and characterization but also thanks to sound design, animation, and art direction.

I should just say right of the bat, so I don't make this review stupdly boring, Gunbuster has quite a few flaws and being the first Hideaki Anno series that's not all too surprising. As you might have guessed by the score I gave these issues do not effect at all my overall enjoyment, but perhaps it's important to point out these problems first. On my first time watching in particular I noticed how jarring and incredibly fast the pacing felt around episode 2 - 3 - 4, which makes a some important character interactions feel a bit rushed. Most noteworthy in this case is between Noriko and her love interest Toren Smith: the two meet during episode 3, they bond each other for about three minutes, only for Smith to meet his demise by the end of the episode. I think this only serves Smith to be seen as a motive or final push for Noriko to become the amazing pilot that she is rather than an interesting character that can be explored just a tad. Jung's relations with her comrades can also be inconsistent at times, as she jumps from being irritating and competitive to friendly and easy-going throughout the three episodes I mentioned.
There's barely if no time at all to explain what the aliens are, what they want and why they attack the human race, the most of what we can tell is that they're giant looking bugs flying in space close to the speed of light.
I would also add that the soundtrack isn't particularly memorable - with the exception of the catchy opening theme and the wonderful, cheerful music heard at the end of the final episode - but, surprisingly, even after my first re-watch, I struggle to recall any other musical themes from the show.

And... that's about all the criticism I can give to TWN. It might be easy for some to complain how much of a crybaby Noriko is or how simple and predictable the plot is with the coach believing in his student despite the latter being terrible with handling the big robots, all of it is fair i suppose but I don't agree with all of this.
Starting with the strongest point of the series; Noriko. I love Noriko, she's the best, plain and simple. I can't express how much I love this girl genuinely, I could spend hundreds of sentences describing just how incredible this protagonist is. First of all, she has amazing personality: being usually calm, sweet tempered and insecure, only to turn to a real fury once she takes control over the Gunbuster. I normally don't understand the criticism that she comes across as too desperate, it seems that anime fans cannot stand seeing characters cry or show any kind of frustration (as often happens with others like Shinji Ikari or Kaiji Itou); it's true that it happens often to Noriko as well, but I found that to be part of her charm. While watching TWN, it felt incredibly rewarding to see the protagonist stand her ground, face the situation with absolute seriousness, unleash the ultimate weapon, and defeat the aliens while maintaining an optimistic attitude. I also found it to be incredibly badass, even though we saw very little of the training she underwent to improve her piloting skills. Whenever I see Noriko worrying about or encouraging those closest to her, I often feel a sense of engagement and fulfillment; and as I continue watching, the tragic loss of her father begins to weigh increasingly heavily.
Now talking about her design, Noriko has an appeal that is both insanely cute and sexy. She shows to have a very "moe" look compared ta least to most characters in Gunbuster, paired with those suits that clearly do not cover most of the legs and thighs. It's obvious that those suits are design to give the viewer a good amount of fanservice, after all Gunbuster, while having a serious and dramatic atmosphere, is also suppose to be dumb fun entertainment, and I'm confident to say the fanservice fits so well in a OVA like this. It's not nearly as obnoxious as some people would like you to believe, it's very natural instead as none of the girls ever shows embarrassment while wearing the suits. As a person who can enjoy fanservice (especially in a Gainax anime) I can say for certain that Noriko is truly peak character design, she looks picture perfect in so many shots.

There are three other characters that contribute a lot to my enjoyment as well.
Ota is the main teacher of the school and later the second-in-command of Exelion, the spaceship used as headquarters for missions in space. Ota completely trusts Noriko and her skills, seeing full potential in her from the very beginning. Koichiro holds Noriko in great esteem and trusts her, making him a trustworthy coach and very interesting guy to follow, especially when his health conditions are getting rough during the second half.
Kazumi Amano is the best student of the school; every girl talks to her with reverence, as Kazumi is definitely a step forward than others. Her abilities nevertheless do not derive form her natural talent but from her continuous diligence and devotion to work and training. She proves to be modest, intelligent, and kind. She becomes friends with Noriko (who looks up to her with admiration) and is ultimately encouraged to fight alongside her.
Jung Freud, member of the Soviet space squadron, is known as a genius of fighting; she comes from the Lunar base and meets Noriko and Kazumi as soon as they arrive to the spaceship Exelion. I know I complained about her personalty being all over the place on occasions, but I ultimately found her rivalry with Kazumi to be fun to watch, it kind of reminds me of Asuka with her cocky and competitive attitude. She will end up having feeling of admiration and compassion for the two companions. In my opinion I find her to be the best looking character in the series along side with Noriko.

The animation and art style have aged beautifully; visually Gunbuster is stunning and a pleasure to watch, and for being a series from the late 80s I had to say the animation was truly cutting-edge, it is mostly fluent save for a few slightly choppy frames. Some of the robots have a pretty generic design but the actual Gubuster itself looks amazing and detailed, and it is imposing when you see it battling in space. Much of the series is filled with vibrant colors and highly detailed backgrounds; the only exception is the final episode, which uses a black-and-white palette. There's a reason it was made like that, at that time Anno was watching Ultraman on a monochrome television that inspired it, and according to Anno himself "The special effects look better in black and white. When you have color, you have an extra dimension of information, color would have gotten in the way of the sense we wanted to portray with a black hole bomb. Also no one had never done it before". Speaking of, the final episode is one of the best things Anno has ever directed - perhaps even one of the best episodes ever - but I prefer not to give any spoilers or say anything about it: just watch it, it is an extraordinary and unforgettable experience.

Well this review is going long enough it seems, might be the longest review Gunbuster has ever seen (on this website at least), time to ramping up my thoughts. It's easy to point out how the story could have developed better if there had been more episodes: simply to explore this universe further, devoting more time to know the characters and understanding the alien species. In a way I felt like I wanted more once I finished episode 6 (which is something that Diebuster did not help in that regard), but after a bit I began to appreciate this OVA for what it is. Given that it was one of Gainax's first successful works, it was guaranteed that it wouldn't be a long-running project spanning 12 or 24 episodes. Even if you might not like Gunbuster, you have to at least respect its existence since it's far more important than some people realize. It's basically a proto-Eva, which I haven't done many comparisons with it because I though there was no need to, but a lot that was created in Gunbuster would later be reshaped in Evangelion and the latter would go on to become one of the most iconic and successful anime of all time.
I recommend Gunbuster to everybody, especially for those curious about the history of Gainax and how this work influenced many other studio's works in the 90s and 2000s. Maybe not everything has aged the best, but it still stands strong and remains at the top!

Sonotame, ikkini ikki mi shitaku naru yōna sakuhinde wa arimasenga, hadede kagekina batorushīn ga sukinara, machigainaku miru kachi wa arimasu. Sore ni, ongaku ga saikō ni kakkoīdesu!

TLDR: Cold, brutal, and dark...is what this anime would have been, but they crammed in what is an anime trope at this point: “Princes publicly dumps the Noble for a commoner” frameset. If you know anime, wysiwyg. The series name says it all. You take a boring but tried and tested formula and try to put a unique twist to it. The not-too-smart arrogant prince gets infatuated by the side pussy, who is a con artist, while being surrounded by moralless nobles willing to break the law to curry a favor. We've all seen or read this a million times. The MC noble girl gets sentback anywhere from 24 hours to 10 years to change things, or someone gets isekaied into her, but they played the game/read the book or insert any asspull cosmic event. Occasionally they get superpowers.

This time around, our MC had no divine intervention but can already beat top-tier knights, uses the highest-level magic, and is a solid businesswoman. It's like she had 5 separate university degrees, masters, and doctorates. Yes, she is Bruce Lee, Einstein, and Jeff Bazos in one Mary Sue. Not only that. She has a faction of people loyal to her that work incognito.

Here is where the plot sort of diverges. Instead of just a poorly paced story littered with long boring dialogue, people get killed. Decapitated, gutted, limbs severed. Not even the children are spared. Love and compassion aren't on the table. The innocent get slaughtered, and there is collateral damage. 

But even with the visceral carnage, they paint it up in the same princess-cutie palette. WTF!
Throw in par animation and VAs, and this show is only acceptable if you switch off your brain for mindless entertainment. This is not entirely bad, but it is far from good.

Yeah, this was absolutely terrible. For a while, I thought the movie was heading toward an ending where the miracles accumulated over the course of the story would finally save both Madoka and Homura — that separating Madoka herself from the Law of Cycles in Rebellion would ultimately turn out to have had a purpose. And I thought, “Well, if you want to save everyone, I guess this is basically the only way to do it.” Then again, Sumaga already did something along those lines back in 2008. But then… what?In the end, are they seriously just going to dump the burden back onto Madoka again?

More elements have been added, the mythology has become more complicated, and there are more moving parts than ever before — but fundamentally, we are right back where we were at the end of the TV series.

So what was the point of these last fifteen years?

And to make matters worse, the movie ends in a way that is blatantly dependent on another sequel.

At some point, this stops feeling like storytelling and starts feeling like the audience is being taken for granted.

Until now, Rebellion was easily the lowest point of Madoka for me. Somehow, this movie managed to go even lower.

At this rate, I honestly expect every new sequel to set a new low.

This may be the worst thing I have ever watched.

Even judged purely as a single film, it is a mess. There are too many ideas, plot devices, characters, concepts, and visual motifs competing for attention. Instead of forming a coherent whole, it feels like a chimera stitched together from several different movies.

The only things I can genuinely praise are the animation and the performances.

Visually, it is impressive. The cast does their job.

But none of that was enough to make the movie work for me.

I am done with this series.

Even if another sequel comes out, I will not be watching it.

data.review: Pure, unfiltered post-irony through panty fanservice. The sheer persistence of these shots transcends the boundaries of conventional fanservice and enters a realm where artistic intent, erotic appeal, and self-aware absurdity become indistinguishable. At some point, the question is no longer whether the camera really needed to be there, but whether the camera itself has become the protagonist. A truly fascinating case study in the relationship between visual storytelling and the unstoppable human urge to look up a skirt. As you can see, this review is marked as a spoiler despite containing not a single word about the plot. And that's precisely the point - the gradual revelation of theshow's post-ironic nature is arguably more important than the plot itself.

Whisper of the Heart (Mimi wo Sumaseba).. During the first half of the film, I kept telling myself that it was just an ordinary movie, and well, in many aspects, it is. However, the idea is executed really well, and the art style plays a big part in that. The world feels alive, full of colour and depth, making it genuinely comforting to look at. However, when you look past the execution, the story itself is just a classic love story. It's predictable, and it's easy to see where things are heading. The characters aren't particularly extraordinary either, nor are they especially deep. But perhaps that'sexactly what makes this film beautiful. It's comforting to watch, doesn't demand much deep thinking, and finds its charm in the simplicity of its story.

Shizuku's passion for books and writing is really nice to see. It's just... ordinary in a beautiful way. Her support for Harada is heartwarming, and the guilt she feels over supposedly messing everything up, despite not really doing anything wrong, her desperation to improve herself in such a short time also shows another side of her. Beneath her energetic exterior, Shizuku is a fragile but deeply caring girl who wants to become someone worthy of her own ambitions and friends.

Seiji, on the other hand, doesn't have much going for him beyond his passion for making violins. A character who starts off as a "jerk" only to turn out nice in the end isn't particularly interesting, and I wish there had been more to his character.

The Baron's story is another really nice touch. I honestly don't know how to put it into words, but there's something beautiful about the hope found in a seemingly impossible wish, as well as the patience and sentiment in Mr. Nishi's heart. It's a small part of the film, yet it adds something genuinely special to it.

8 nyans out of 10.

Bro Thinks He's the Fourth Member of the Big Three 💀 I'm not even going to lie, watching *Black Torch* feels like watching someone who just finished *Naruto*, *Bleach*, and *Jujutsu Kaisen* decide to become a mangaka overnight. Bro took notes from all three, changed a few names, threw in a cat, and thought he had cooked something revolutionary. My guy, the kitchen is on fire, and the fire itself is more original than this plot. Let's talk about the protagonist first. Another delinquent guy with a special ability who gets dragged into the supernatural world? Wow. I've definitely never seen that before. Oh wait, Ichigo exists.Yuji exists. And about a thousand other shonen protagonists exist. At this point, creating a generic shonen MC should be a school assignment because apparently everyone is passing with full marks.

Then we get the supernatural stuff. Spirits, powers, secret organizations, supernatural fights — the usual package. *Black Torch* really said, "What if we took the general vibe of *Bleach*, added some *Jujutsu Kaisen* seasoning, sprinkled a little *Naruto* on top, and hoped nobody tasted the difference?"

Brother, I can taste the entire recipe.

The most hilarious part is how familiar everything feels. You know that feeling when you start a new anime and spend the entire episode thinking about three other anime you've already watched? That's *Black Torch*. Instead of making me curious about its own world, it keeps reminding me of the shows that did similar things before it. I'm watching one series and mentally opening tabs for three others.

And before someone comes at me with the classic "every anime copies something," yes, obviously. Nobody expects every mangaka to descend from the heavens with an idea that has never existed in human history. Tropes are normal. Inspiration is normal. But there's a difference between using familiar tropes and making your entire identity feel like a second-hand purchase.

*Naruto* has its ninja world, rivalries, and emotional character arcs. *Bleach* has its distinctive style and spiritual mythology. *Jujutsu Kaisen* has its own take on modern supernatural combat. You can criticize these series all day, but at least they have recognizable identities.

Meanwhile, *Black Torch* sometimes feels like it walked into a shonen convention, stole everyone's homework, changed the handwriting, and submitted it five minutes before the deadline.

And the cat. Yes, the cat. I'm not saying the cat is bad, but the fact that a cat is part of the hook feels like the author desperately needed something to make the pitch sound different. "Guys, hear me out. What if we had supernatural powers... BUT THERE'S A CAT?"

Absolute cinema, apparently.

The frustrating thing is that the premise could have been interesting. A delinquent who can interact with supernatural beings? There is room to do something cool with that. You could build an interesting relationship between the characters, explore the supernatural world, or create a combat system that feels unique.

But having potential and actually doing something with it are two different things. A bag of ingredients isn't a meal, and a collection of shonen tropes isn't automatically a good shonen anime.

The entire thing gives me the energy of a student who studied three previous exam papers, memorized all the answers, and walked into the exam thinking they were a genius. Sure, you might pass, but don't expect me to call you Einstein.

And honestly, that's my biggest problem with *Black Torch*. It isn't necessarily that the ideas are bad. It's that the series struggles to make them feel fresh. Instead of making me say, "Damn, that's an interesting concept," it makes me say, "Oh, so we're doing this again?"

We've got supernatural entities. We've got a rebellious protagonist. We've got special abilities. We've got stylish fights. We've got the whole shonen starter pack.

Where's the personality, bro? Where's the secret ingredient? Did the originality budget get cut during production?

At some point, you have to stop collecting other anime's leftovers and start cooking your own meal.

### Final verdict

*Black Torch* feels like a fanfiction that accidentally got a production budget. It's got pieces that remind me of *Naruto*, *Bleach*, and *Jujutsu Kaisen*, but reminding me of better-known anime isn't the same as giving me a reason to care about your own.

Could it entertain people? Sure. Is it automatically trash because it uses familiar tropes? No. But does it deserve to be treated like some groundbreaking new shonen masterpiece? Absolutely not.

This anime walked so generically that even its shadow looks like a recycled character design.

**My final message to Black Torch:** Bro, you don't need to reinvent shonen, but at least give us a reason to remember your name without mentioning three other anime first.

Because right now, *Black Torch* isn't beating the copycat allegations. It's walking into court wearing a Naruto headband, carrying Ichigo's sword, and asking Gojo to represent it.

Case closed. 💀

I am really glad I watched this. Almost everything that frustrated me about the TV series works much better here. The biggest difference is simple: the movie no longer needs to introduce nine characters and their relationships from scratch. It can use everything the TV series established and go straight into the conflicts that were left unfinished. Mahiru’s feelings toward Hikari finally receive proper attention. Maya and Claudine get the confrontation they always deserved. And most importantly for me, Banana gets a lot more to do. The train sequence was exactly the Banana I wanted to see. Her warmth, menace, confidence, and theatricality all come together there. It was easilyone of my favorite parts of the film.

The revues are also far stronger than they were in the TV series.

In the series, they sometimes felt compressed because each episode also had to handle setup and plot progression. Here, the revue itself becomes the drama. Music, dialogue, movement, editing, and stage imagery all express the relationships directly.

The film also benefits from being much more willing to abandon ordinary realism. A train can become a stage, a conversation can become a duel, and emotion can reshape the entire space around the characters.

That abstraction does not make the film harder to understand. If anything, it makes the emotions clearer.

The TV series had great characters and ideas, but often felt too cramped to use them fully.

The movie finally gives those ideas enough room to breathe.

This was the Revue Starlight I wanted to see.

This is basically BanG Dream! SEED DESTINY. My first impression was that the script simply was not refined enough. It tries to do too many things at once, and the result feels scattered. More than anything, I disliked how the dramatic pressure and tension could never sustain themselves for very long. Around episode 2, I was thinking: “This is hell… and there are still ten more episodes of this? Excellent.”I genuinely expected the story to keep descending from there.

But around the “Haruhikage” incident and the reunion, the pressure suddenly dropped.

That was a major disappointment for me.

The developments themselves make sense on a plot level. My problem is that the drama leading to them did not feel convincing enough.

Instead of watching relationships gradually reach a breaking point, I often felt like I was simply watching a sequence of events happen because the story needed to move on.

The series also relies far too heavily on Mortis to push the plot forward.

Because Mortis is given so much narrative agency, Sakiko often ends up feeling less like a character and more like a device that the story moves around.

Her material involving Hatsune is one of the exceptions, and I wish the series had given her more scenes with that level of personal weight.

Episodes 11 and 12 finally gave me a sense of:

“Oh, this is what I wanted.”

But by then, it was too late.

If the ideas and tension from those episodes had been woven into the middle of the series instead of being saved for the end, I think the whole thing could have been much stronger.

There is good material here.

I just do not think it was assembled into the best possible shape.

Textbook "it's fine". It's not offensively bad or boring and it has more going for it than it does against it, thus the score. The plot: meh. Decent character progression, afaic the Mewi bits were far and away the best part of the plot this season. Animation and visuals: good, it's what held up the best coming from season 1. Fight choreography remains very good. Sound: ffs the sound mixing is AWFUL to the point it nearly ruined the watching experience for me. Inner monologues sound like the characters are talking from the other end of a tunnel, the audience KNOWS what an inner monologue is and doesn'tneed that extra effect added. Volume is a mess in general, there are fight scenes where the sound effects and music are so overblown you either go deaf or need to set the volume at nearly half what you would for any normal show, and you turn the characters' voices into whispers in the process since the volume for that part of the mix is correct unlike the rest. Sound effects themselves are as good as in any show, the ost is good, voice acting is good, the individual bits range from competent to properly good - it's the sound mixing that's offensively bad. Please ffs either teach whoever did it not to suck, or get someone else for season 3. Oh btw, my thing is photography, not music... So it's not like I'm being a snob because I'm overly invested in this part of anime production. The sound was just *that bad*, it's actually what prompted me to write a review in the first place... which I think says it all.

Overall this season sort of feels like... not like filler because that's not what "filler" means, but it feels like it's bland at its core and it's mostly meant to connect what happened in season 1 to whatever's coming next. And that kind of "bridge" material usually doesn't happen until later in a story, when way more stuff has happened and the story needs to get some room for a shift in tone or a transition to an entirely different focal point in the overall plot. This? I wonder what's happening in season 3 and beyond, maybe the whole story is more a simmer than a boil lol.

I cannot say for certain what Alien 9 is ultimately trying to say, but this is how I interpreted it. To me, it is a story about the fear of growing up. Joining the Alien Countermeasures Committee and being forced to coexist with the Borg felt like entering the adult world: becoming part of an organization, being assigned responsibilities, and having no choice but to adapt. What makes it frightening is that the girls are never truly ready for any of this. The world simply demands that they accept it. Even the Borg feels symbolic in that sense. It is something foreign that attaches itself to the body and eventuallybecomes part of everyday life.

Growing up here is not liberation.

It is being incorporated into a system and changed by it.

And no one is coming to save you.

That is what stayed with me most.

Strongest exorcist isn’t slop. It isn’t even less than slop. It’s whatever is below that. Every. Single. Thing. About this anime doesn’t matter. Not the previous life. Not the side characters. Not the enemies. Not the stakes. Not the romance. All of it is trivial, and never matters. You see a bad guy? No you don’t. He’s gone. You like that romance? Well we forgot that we had that. This persons super strong? That doesn’t matter anymore, and we forget. You want to see an epic fight? No you don’t. It’s over. So what does it have…? Do you like an annoying side character thatyou forget the name of immediately that spends the entire anime complaining for no reason just to be told to shut up and get wiped from the writing? Well we have that. Do you like interesting enemies that have 7 seconds of screen time before never appearing again? We have that. Do you like boring archetypes of characters that are never consistent? We have that. Oh don’t forget the tropey hook of the mc being hated. But actually. Do forget it. Gone. 

The art and fights are average at best. The characters are poorly written and never given any depth past the archetype they are. Our mc never grows or gains any sort of development. This is a bad experience. One you can’t even laugh at, as it takes itself too seriously. 

To the very end you might think “oh, maybe it’ll wrap itself up. Maybe I can just say it was decent slop and call it a day.” But even the ending, like everything in this entire awful waste of time, is lacking any semblance of closure, substance, or direction. This isn’t an anime. It’s a weapon you aim at someone. Give this recommendation to someone to upset them, waste their time, or test them. 

This anime gets my award for most pointless story of all time.

My first thought after finishing the TV series was simple: Twelve episodes were not enough. This story needed two cours. And more importantly, nine main characters are simply too many for a twelve-episode series. There is not enough time to properly develop all of them, and as a result, the series often feels distracted. It wants to explore Karen and Hikari, Banana, Maya and Claudine, Mahiru, Junna, Futaba and Kaoruko — but there simply is not enough room for everyone. If the series absolutely had to be twelve episodes, I think it might have been stronger if it had sacrificed some of the supporting cast and focused much more heavilyon Karen and Hikari.

The same problem affects the revue scenes.

Because each episode has to introduce a conflict, develop it, and then reach a revue within roughly twenty minutes, the revue sequences themselves often feel too short. The songs are important to the concept of the series, but many of them did not leave as strong an impression on me as I wanted them to.

The whole series feels like it has excellent material, but not enough time to cook it properly.

That said, the characters themselves are fantastic.

My favorite is Banana.

I am extremely weak to the type of cheerful, dependable character who turns out to have something much stranger going on underneath the surface.

I am an otaku. Of course I am.

That is also why my frustration with the TV series is stronger than it otherwise would have been. The ingredients are clearly there. The cast is good, the visual ideas are strong, the theatrical concept is unique, and there are moments where the series becomes genuinely fascinating.

I just kept thinking there was a better version of this material that the twelve-episode format could not fully reach.

The true strength of TEXHNOLYZE is that its second half completely changes the meaning of its first. The cold atmosphere that runs through the entire series, the restrained direction that rarely explains things through dialogue, and the setting of Lux are all incredibly compelling. But to be honest, the first half of the story itself did not impress me that much. The conflict surrounding Yoshii and the various factions felt fairly conventional. After twelve episodes, I still could not understand why this anime had continued to be discussed for so many years. Then the second half began.And that is where I understood.

TEXHNOLYZE is beautiful when it collapses.

Once Kano enters the story, everything begins to fall apart as if the entire world has suddenly started accelerating downward.

Organizations collapse. Relationships collapse. The city collapses. The assumptions the viewer had built up about this world begin collapsing with them.

And this is exactly why the first half becomes necessary.

Its slowness is not meaningless.

The first half establishes a world that, despite being bleak and abnormal, still possesses a structure. There are factions, power struggles, routines, ambitions, and people trying to preserve some kind of order.

The second half destroys all of it.

If the world had been broken from the very beginning, I probably would have simply thought, “What a strange and miserable place.”

But because the series spends so much time establishing its world before taking it apart, the collapse has weight.

The first half becomes the preparation for the fall.

And in retrospect, that changes how I see everything that came before it.

Of all the portrayals of collapse I have seen in anime, this is the one that has felt the most convincing to me.

And also the most beautiful.

I understand why the division now. It's not great and cuts a ton of corners. Searching for a new romance anime THIS IS IT! Stop whatever you are doing and give this show the time of day. This show has the perfect combination of amazing soundtrack, moving story, lots of adorable moments, and most of all dynamic side characters. EVERY character even ones with little screen feel real and fleshed out. Each one is introduced organically like they have been there all along. Show is similar to Horimiya where their love develops as the relationship continues and learn more about each other. HOWEVER, you get 2 other very flushed out relationships. The pacing is fast and I LOVE IT! Noslow drawn out cultural festival planning or sports festival moments. It's shown, but not in a way that makes it an entire arc. Like in any normal high school moment not every event has something dramatic happen, sometimes the only interaction you get is a photo taken together and thats it. Every student has jobs which I find unique and illustrates how each individual character has depth. Not just the MC has a quirky part time job because everyone needs money and some have other plans. Resulting in interesting new friend dynamics. 

I don't know what else to type to convince you, but you will be hooked by the first episode and you won't stop. Haven't seen the sub, but dub is the WAY TO GO!

This is a surprisingly difficult movie to talk about. I neither like it nor dislike it. The main reason I cannot really say I like it is simple: I do not think it works as a story in the first place. It feels more like a music video that has been given something resembling a narrative framework. And because of that, the parts I enjoyed the most were exactly the parts where it stopped pretending otherwise.The live-performance sequences were good.
The “ray” music video was good.

Those are the moments where the film feels most comfortable with what it actually wants to be.

While watching it, I also kept thinking about some of the criticism I had seen beforehand — complaints about how implausible the protagonist’s circumstances were, or how conveniently the conflict with her mother was resolved.

And all I could think was:

Are we really starting there?

To me, this movie never even reaches the point where those kinds of criticisms become particularly meaningful.

It is like standing in a room with an elephant in the middle of it and complaining about the color of the wallpaper.

Whether a particular character motivation is realistic or whether a dramatic resolution is too convenient seems almost irrelevant when the larger issue is that the film barely functions according to conventional narrative logic at all.

Some works simply are not meant to be received head-on.

You have to let them pass by you from the side.

Trying to force this movie into the framework of a conventional drama only makes the discussion stranger.

At the same time, that is also why I cannot say I dislike it.

The lack of substance feels intentional.

The movie seems perfectly aware that it is built around music, images, atmosphere, and spectacle first, with narrative existing mainly as connective tissue.

And I can respect that more than a film that half-heartedly tries to become a serious “story” without fully committing to it.

If you are going to be empty, being this completely and deliberately empty is at least a coherent choice.

I do not think Chou Kaguya-hime! is a good story.

I am not even sure it is particularly interested in being one.

And once I accepted that, the movie became much easier to understand.

The story itself isn't anything notable, a generic romantic supernatural comedy but the way its presented i quite enjoy. Again im probably bias as ive always had a soft spot for anime like this. You know those anime that make you think: “Ah, this show does not actually have much to say. It just wants to look deep.” Ergo Proxy feels like the undiluted essence of that kind of anime. Pure pretentiousness. I started getting suspicious when I noticed things like the use of Radiohead for the ending theme and the constant references to philosophers and philosophical terminology.And somehow, my suspicion turned out to be completely correct.

What is impressive about Ergo Proxy is that even most supposedly “pretentious” anime usually have some kind of narrative core underneath all the symbolism. There is normally at least a central idea, theme, or argument that the presentation is built around.

Here, I barely felt any of that.

It feels like 100% aesthetic posturing.

Names, symbols, quotations, religious imagery, philosophy, obscure dialogue, deliberately confusing structure — everything is arranged to create the sensation that something profound must be hiding underneath.

But the more I watched, the more I felt that the sensation itself was the entire point.

And strangely enough, I do not even dislike the anime for that.

There is something almost admirable about how completely it commits to the act. It never breaks character. It never becomes embarrassed by its own seriousness. It just keeps going.

So rather than making me angry, it eventually became fascinating.

I also think the reputation surrounding this series can be misleading. It is often treated as if its obscurity and philosophical references automatically make it intellectually substantial.

I do not think they do.

Complexity, ambiguity, references, and difficult presentation are not the same thing as depth.

If anything, Ergo Proxy is an excellent vaccine against confusing “something that looks profound” with “something that actually is profound.”

For that reason alone, I almost recommend watching it.

Not because I think it is a great anime, but because it is an unusually useful viewing experience.

Once you have seen something this concentrated, you may become much better at recognizing the same tricks elsewhere.

First, I should clarify that this is not really a review of Season 4 alone. It is a review of the series as a whole, based on how I felt after watching all 85 episodes up through Season 4. After spending this much time with Re:ZERO, I finally realized what my fundamental problem with the series is: I simply do not get along with its obsession with depicting everything in extreme detail. And by “detailed,” I do not necessarily mean “carefully crafted.” For the amount of time the series spends on its story, the payoff often feels surprisingly small. Re:ZERO takes its time depicting conversations, psychology, relationships, worldbuilding,and every intermediate step in great detail. This certainly gives the story a sense of reality and density, and as an adaptation trying to preserve the texture of the original light novels, I think it is largely successful.

But as an anime, I am much less convinced.

Detail does not automatically create depth. To me, it can sometimes feel like drawing Doraemon as an absurdly muscular character in an ultra-detailed gekiga style: technically, there is much more information on the screen, but that does not necessarily make the underlying material any richer.

Season 3 was so packed with events that this tendency was partially hidden. The sheer amount of material forced the anime to compress things, and I actually think the series benefited from that.

Season 4 made the problem much more obvious.

After 19 episodes, my reaction was basically: “That’s it?”

The memory-loss plotline does work as a way of showing how much Subaru has grown compared to the person he used to be. I understand what the arc is trying to accomplish, and in isolation I think it succeeds.

But after 85 episodes, the result still feels strangely modest compared to the enormous amount of time invested in getting there.

There are other anime that manage to express a comparable amount of character development, thematic progression, and emotional change in roughly 24 episodes. Re:ZERO instead seems committed to documenting almost every step of the journey.

For people who value that accumulation of detail, this may be exactly what makes the series special.

For me, however, it increasingly feels like narrative inefficiency rather than richness.

If Re:ZERO continues with this same approach, I honestly do not know whether I will keep watching.
